lesson.title: Count to Infinity: When Good News Travels Fast and Bad News Travels Slow
lesson.summary: Count to infinity is a failure mode in distance vector routing where, after a link goes down, routers can keep exchanging and incrementing a stale distance estimate through each other instead of quickly recognizing that the destination is unreachable.
lesson.body:
Distance vector routing's great strength, that a router only needs to trust what its neighbors tell it, is also the source of its worst failure mode. A router has no way to independently verify a neighbor's claim to reach some destination, it can only take the claim, add its own link cost, and believe the result. That works well when link costs only ever improve or stay the same. It works badly when a link fails, because a stale, outdated piece of good news can circulate between routers, each one unaware that the other's information is now out of date, each one making the number look worse rather than making it disappear.

Walk through the classic three router case to see exactly how this happens. Routers A, B, and C sit in a line, A connected to B, B connected to C, every link at cost 1. Before anything goes wrong, B has a direct route to A at cost 1, and C, having learned from B, has a route to A at cost 2, 1 to reach B, plus B's cost of 1 to reach A. Now the A to B link fails. B, directly attached to that link, notices immediately and removes its direct route to A. But before B can tell C about the failure, C sends its regular update, still advertising the old, stale information, that it can reach A at cost 2.

B receives that stale advertisement and, having no way to know it is stale, applies the ordinary distance vector rule: cost to reach C, 1, plus C's advertised cost to A, 2, totals 3, which looks like a real route since B's own direct route is now gone. B adopts it, distance to A is now 3, by way of C. B then advertises this to C. C, applying the same rule with no way to know B's 3 traces back to C's own earlier claim, computes 1, to reach B, plus 3, B's new claim, for a total of 4, and updates its own table to 4, still supposedly by way of B. C then re-advertises 4 back to B, B recomputes 1 plus 4 equals 5, and the cycle continues, each router unknowingly feeding the other's stale number back to itself, the distance climbing one hop's worth at a time.

This is count to infinity: the correct, immediate answer, that A is unreachable, is delayed by round after round of routers politely trusting each other's outdated advertisements, with the estimated distance climbing slowly instead of collapsing quickly. In a protocol like RIP, this loop is not infinite in practice, because RIP treats 16 as infinity, once the climbing count reaches 16, both routers finally mark A unreachable and the loop ends. But reaching 16 can take many rounds of updates, during which packets addressed to A are actively routed in a circle between B and C rather than being dropped immediately, wasting bandwidth and delaying the network's recovery. The two techniques covered next, split horizon and poison reverse, exist specifically to shrink or shortcut this problem.
